Morning people make me sick. Some people just get up at 5 am naturally, fluff their hair once, sit outside on their balcony and sing with the birds for a bit, and then lunge into instant productivity. Meanwhile God, in his infinite wisdom, thought it right to make my most productive hours between 11pm and 4am. It’s not fair. However, after trying every sleep app on the app store, sunrise clocks, youtube videos, and alarms that make you do math and squats to turn them off, I believe I’ve reached some sort of enlightenment. I finally have a morning routine worth following to make mornings less of a slog. And I’d like to share that routine with you, along with some tips. Let’s get started.

### 1\. Disable the Snooze button

This is a big one. I’ve learned that it doesn’t matter how many minutes later you set it, the snooze button is never helpful. The promises of the snooze button are a lie by big Alarm Clock™ to make waking up seem less miserable. In reality, the shallow transient sleep you get in the 5–30mins you snoozed will not make you feel more rested or give you more energy. In fact, you’ll interrupt your natural sleep cycle and wake up in the middle, not at the tail end, like you would if you woke up naturally. You will wake up more miserable. Here’s the truth. No amount of snoozing is going to make waking up better. Waking up sucks. Do not negotiate with your mind on this one. Move your alarm clock across the room so you have to walk to go get it. And when your alarm clock goes off, keep your eyes open, even if you need to stay in the bed for a bit, and then get up and turn the alarm clock off. When you turn it off, you’re up, end of discussion. Start the rest of your routine.

### 2\. Use light exercise to jump start your brain

When you first wake up, your brain is still in low power mode, which is part of what’s making you feel miserable. You can fix this by giving your brain a little juice (in this case oxygen). Some light exercise can get your heart pumping and send your brain lots of oxygen to get the little guy up and at ‘em. This doesn’t have to be a full workout, the goal is not to improve your body, but to wake up your brain. 10–15 mins is good enough. For me, this used to look like push ups and jumping jacks, but it turns out the neighbors below me weren’t as jazzed about me bettering myself at 5am (how rude). Now, on someone’s recommendation, I’ve taken up short morning yoga, which works well for getting the blood pumping and working through morning stiffness.¹

### 3\. The Cold Shower

This is the one part of a morning routine that everyone consistently recommended and which I consistently ignored. For a couple reasons. First, who wants to spend their shower miserable? I love hot showers, they give me time to decompress and think. I don’t want to spend that time shivering and cursing the day I was born. Second, I feel like The Cold Shower has become emblematic of / synonymous with optimization culture and the routines of brofluincers who record themselves in the morning racing cars on foot with weighted jackets and eating bull testes for the “health benefits”. For these reasons, The Cold Shower made me cringe. However, I was convinced by a funny, but helpful youtube video to give it a try.² What convinced me was the thought that this doesn’t have to be my long shower. The goal is to just let the water cover your body and hit you for 20–30 seconds. In and out. I was surprised by how much energy you come out of the shower with and that’s what finally sold me on doing it consistently. Before I get in, I typically smack my face and say a lot of cheesy anime and movie quotes that make me grateful I live alone.

### 4\. Reflection and aiming yourself

This part of the routine is going to vary by person, but you need something to ground yourself for the day. If you think of yourself as an arrow, this is the part of the routine that sets your trajectory for launching into the rest of your day. I’m Christian, so for me this looks like prayer, reading, and silent reflection. Particularly, I’ve been praying the Daily Office from the Book of Common Prayer.³ It’s important that this part of your routine be done in silence, alone, and with intention. The things I think about during this part of the routine often become the things that I meditate and ruminate on throughout the rest of my day. So fill this time with meaningful and life giving material.

### 5\. Chart your course for the day

This is the one part of the routine that I’m okay skipping, but I still think it’s worth talking about. This is where you orient yourself by looking at your calendar for the next few days, your running to-do list, and write your to-dos for the day. This could be its’ own separate post, but ideally, you should have a running list of your to-dos, broken out into the major categories of your life, that you can reference. You pull from this list based on what’s most pressing and add it to your particular to-dos for that day. I’ve tried many different to-do apps and I’ve finally settled on these list just being simple text. My running to-do list is a pinned apple note with a check list and my daily to-dos are hand-written in a to-dos journal. You should pick no more than three important to-dos for the day. It’s important that you’re realistic about your day and pick to-dos that can actually be done considering everything else you have going on, though it’s okay if something rolls to another day. If you already have one or two big things that are pressing and you know you have to do them today, you don’t really need the to-do list, and that’s often when I skip writing that and just check my calendar.

### 6\. Immediately start doing the thing

After writing your to-dos, you should now have several items to…well..to do. Start doing one of them. Tell yourself that you’re just going to put a little effort into moving the ball forward. Likely, your brain juices will get flowing and you’ll keep working on whatever it is until you put some significant progress in. This post itself is a product of me launching into an idea immediately in the morning. And no matter what kind of progress you put into the task, it’s an automatic win because the flow of a day often snowballs. You start the day working on what needs to be done and you’re more likely to continue that trend throughout the rest of your day. The sense of accomplishment from putting in meaningful work will carry you.

### Closing thoughts and final tips

A good morning is like a smile from a loved one, it just makes you feel good. Even if you don’t get anything meaningful done, even if the rest of your day sucks, even if you’re not a morning person, a good morning is a gift. I know not everyone’s work or personal schedules can accommodate for early mornings, but I hope you were able to find something in this post worth incorporating to help you experience the gift of a good morning. I’m going to throw down below a shotgun blast of other helpful tips that I couldn’t find a place for, but felt worth mentioning. Thanks for reading.

-   **No fast dopamine activities:** Notice how during this routine I mentioned nothing about a phone. That was on purpose. Activities like scrolling, checking notifications, and short video watching are fast dopaminic activities. They give you a fast hit and afterward, your body has to lower its’ dopamine levels to balance you out. This means doing these kind of activities are not only a distraction, but actually drain you of the resources you need to want to do the kind of slow-dopaminic activities that the best mornings are made of (meditation, reflection, and creative work). Mornings are an A and B conversation between you and your body. Tell your phone to C its’ way out.

-   **No caffeine for the first few hours after waking up:** It turns out your body has its’ own chemical goodies for waking you up, cortisol. Your body starts ramping up production as you’re waking up and this is all kicked off by your circadian rhythm, which tries to guess when you’re gonna wake up. Let your body do it’s job and wake you up itself before you dip into the caffeine. If you go for the caffeine immediately, you train your body out of producing more cortisol to wake you up in a way that feels good.

-   **Do your routine outside of your bedroom:** The bedroom is mainly for sleeping (among other things). Do not attempt to do your routine, your reading, your work, from within your bedroom, that’s not going to work. Go to your office or balcony. On those harder mornings, you may even need to leave the house
